cards.explanation: The answer is a mighty king. The Teacher says he “…came against it, surrounded it, and built large siege ramps against it.” (Ecclesiastes 9:14) Few men inside, one big king outside. That is a lopsided day.

The answer is a poor wise man. “Now a poor wise man was found in the city, and he saved the city by his wisdom.” (Ecclesiastes 9:15) Wisdom did the saving. I like that, friends, because wisdom doesn't need a big budget.

The answer is False. He saved the city by his wisdom, “Yet no one remembered that poor man.” (Ecclesiastes 9:15) Saving a whole city and not being remembered is hard to hear. I know a little about being forgotten, and I think the Teacher is noticing something real.

The answer is that people despise his wisdom and ignore his words. The Teacher says “Wisdom is better than strength, but the wisdom of the poor man is despised, and his words are not heeded.” (Ecclesiastes 9:16) Wisdom wins, yet the man holding it gets the cold shoulder. Both things are true at once.

The answer is True, friends. “The calm words of the wise are heeded over the shouts of a ruler among fools.” (Ecclesiastes 9:17) Calm beats loud in this verse. And I say that as a stamper who loves being loud.

The word is destroys. “Wisdom is better than weapons of war, but one sinner destroys much good.” (Ecclesiastes 9:18) One person can wreck a lot. It's a little like one dropped tray ruining a whole batch.

The point is that a little folly outweighs wisdom and honor. “As dead flies bring a stench to the perfumer’s oil, so a little folly outweighs wisdom and honor.” (Ecclesiastes 10:1) The dead flies bring a stench to the oil. A little folly does the same to wisdom and honor.

The answer is False. Even as the fool walks along the road, “…his sense is lacking, and he shows everyone that he is a fool.” (Ecclesiastes 10:3) He isn't hiding anything. He's basically wearing a sign.

The word is calmness, friends. “If the ruler’s temper flares against you, do not abandon your post, for calmness lays great offenses to rest.” (Ecclesiastes 10:4) The ruler's temper is hot, so the answer is the opposite. Stay steady where you are.

What the Teacher has seen is slaves on horseback and princes on foot. “I have seen slaves on horseback, while princes go on foot like slaves.” (Ecclesiastes 10:7) He calls it an evil he has seen under the sun, an error from the ruler (Ecclesiastes 10:5). Everything is flipped.

The answer is True, friends. “The one who quarries stones may be injured by them, and he who splits logs endangers himself.” (Ecclesiastes 10:9) Every job has its risks, even the ones that look simple. Splitting logs is right there on the Teacher's list. Let's all respect the log splitters.

The answer is skill. “If the axe is dull and the blade unsharpened, more strength must be exerted, but skill produces success.” (Ecclesiastes 10:10) Pushing harder isn't the same as working smarter. The sharp thinking does the job.

The answer is False, friends. “If the snake bites before it is charmed, there is no profit for the charmer.” (Ecclesiastes 10:11) When the bite comes first, the charmer gets no profit. Timing matters, and he comes up empty.

The word is consume, friends. “The words of a wise man’s mouth are gracious, but the lips of a fool consume him.” (Ecclesiastes 10:12) Gracious words on one side, consuming lips on the other. A fool's own talk eats him up.

The fool's talk starts foolish and ends even worse. “The beginning of his talk is folly, and the end of his speech is evil madness.” (Ecclesiastes 10:13) It starts bad and gets worse. Keep talking and the hole gets deeper.

The answer is False, friends. “No one knows what is coming, and who can tell him what will come after him?” (Ecclesiastes 10:14) The question leaves the fool with no one to tell him. Nobody can see ahead, and the fool still multiplies words.

The reason is that he does not know the way to the city, friends. “The toil of a fool wearies him, for he does not know the way to the city.” (Ecclesiastes 10:15) The text says he toils and he does not know the way. I bet that is exhausting.

The princes feast for strength and not for drunkenness. The Teacher says “Blessed are you, O land whose king is a son of nobles, and whose princes feast at the proper time…” (Ecclesiastes 10:17) The verse goes on to say the feast is for strength and not for drunkenness. The princes feast at the proper time, and the verse calls that land blessed.

The two words are laziness and idle, friends. “Through laziness the roof caves in, and in the hands of the idle, the house leaks.” (Ecclesiastes 10:18) The verse puts laziness right at the cause. Little jobs left undone add up, and idle hands mean a leaky house. The drip adds up.

The reason is that a bird of the air may carry your words. “Do not curse the king even in your thoughts, or curse the rich even in your bedroom, for a bird of the air may carry your words, and a winged creature may report your speech.” (Ecclesiastes 10:20) Even private words can travel. The verse names a bird of the air and a winged creature.
